newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba's Jochimsen, Welteke split on EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba's Jochimsen, Welteke split on EMU delay.

text.p: Members of Germany's Bundesbank council clashed on Monday over whether Europe's monetary union (EMU) should go ahead on time, with one saying delay in the project would be preferable to having a soft euro.

Council member Reimut Jochimsen said the prospect of a weakling European currency was worse than a move to hold the project up, while his colleague Ernst Welteke said talk of delay was damaging to the German economy and threatened to aggravate unemployment.

In the introduction to the annual report for the State Central Bank of Hessen, Welteke said the euro would not be a weak currency and would be more stable than the mark against non-EMU currencies such as the yen and the dollar.
"The discussion about delaying the euro's introduction should be judged as negative. A delay would help neither the German economy nor its workers," Welteke wrote.

But, addressing a news conference in Duesseldorf, Jochimsen rejected a recent statement by Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, who said the point of no return for starting monetary union had already been reached.
"I believe the point of no return will not be reached until 1998," said Jochimsen, who is also president of the state central bank of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Taking 1997 economic and fiscal performance as a base, the the European Union (EU) is due make the final decision in spring 1998 on which countries qualify for monetary union, scheduled to be launched in 1999.

Jochimsen warned against softening EMU entry rules to allow a large group of countries to take part in the first wave and said awareness was waning of the need for a strict application of the convergence criteria.
"Solid material foundations for monetary union are indispensable," he said.

"If after the start of monetary union it turns out that the foundations do not yet support -- if the euro either fails, drifts apart, or becomes a weak currency -- the damage to European integration would be far worse than for example a limited and conditional postponement."

While Jochimsen said recent volatility in financial markets stemmed in part from uncertainty over whether the choice of EMU first-rounders will be a political or an economic decision, Welteke argued the jitters were prompted by constant talk of a possible delay to the project.
This unsettled atmosphere would in turn hamper Germany's ability to meet the entry criteria, Welteke said, since the flight-to-quality it prompted would boost the mark and bruise German exports.
He said the Maastricht treaty allowed room for interpretation on fiscal convergence criteria.
German efforts to meet the EMU deficit goal are being hindered by stinging unemployment levels which are draining large cash flows from the government's coffers.

A further blow is likely to come later this week, when the government's 1997 May tax estimates are released. Many independent analysts say the estimates will show a shortfall of up to 20 billion marks.

Welteke said joblessness was currently one of EU's critical issues, and while EMU would not solve the problem, which his said was largely structural, it would improve prospects for economic growth and job creation.
"(EMU) is therefore not only in the interests of the Germany economy but also in those of its workers," he said.

Jochimsen, on the other hand, warned against a hasty start to the project, saying any interpretation of the Maastricht rules should not be generous and warning against the use of creative accounting to qualify for the first round.
He also attacked the EU Commission for reportedly paying experts to play down the risks involved in adopting the euro.

"If the EU Commission, as recently reported in the press, makes a whole series of secret arrangements with 170 scientists and high-ranking experts to talk down the risks under the pretext of giving objective information and in return for payment from EU funds ... that is most definitely not the right way to solve the problem ..." he said.
